  <entry>
    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28763v1</id>
    <title>Who Is Prompt-Injecting Coding Agents? An Empirical Study of Hidden AI-Directed Text on GitHub</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T12:15:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28763v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28763v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>AI coding agents now triage issues, review pull requests and pick up tasks inside GitHub repositories, and to do so they read text that anyone with a GitHub account can write. This makes GitHub a prime surface for indirect prompt injection, in which instructions embedded in untrusted content steer a model that later processes it. Prior work has demonstrated such attacks against agents on GitHub in controlled settings, but how often they occur in practice, who deploys them, and for what purpose remain unknown.
  We present the first large-scale empirical study of AI-directed hidden text on GitHub. We analyzed roughly 145 million issues, pull requests, comments and README files, detected text that GitHub does not render to a human reader but that an agent receives in full, and filtered it with a two-stage LLM classification, a template provenance check and an exhaustive manual review. We identify 2,281 validated findings in issues, pull requests and comments (16 per million items), and AI-directed hidden text in the READMEs of 107 repositories.
  We find a heterogeneous ecosystem of four uses: attacks on other parties' agents, defensive text that restricts agents, content override that steers what they write, and first-party orchestration, in which projects coordinate their own agents through hidden markers. Attacks are rare (about one in 3.3 million items) but aimed at maintainers' own triage, review and CI agents. Orchestration accounts for two thirds of the findings in issues, pull requests and comments, grew fivefold in four months, and forms a control channel that anyone who can comment can imitate. Replayed offline against five models we tested, the attacks succeed against one small, fast model in 19% of cases, and against none once HTML comments are stripped. We release our detection tool and every finding.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28173v1</id>
    <title>Selective Verification in Multi-Agent Orchestration with Large Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T04:42:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28173v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28173v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agents can agree because they relied on the same flawed evidence. We use an exact model of nine binary votes to examine when a verifier should intervene. In the main comparison, workers err 20 percent of the time under ordinary conditions, shared failures occur in 10 percent of cases, and the verifier errs 2 percent of the time in either state. When worker error during a shared failure is 80 percent, checking close votes yields 7.93 percent verdict error, compared with 9.06 percent for random checks at the same expected check rate. The ordering reverses at 90 percent worker error during failure. At the matched check rate for that regime, checking close votes yields 9.98 percent error, random checks yield 9.41 percent, and ranking checks by their expected error reduction yields 6.73 percent. The model also shows that passing branch vote counts preserves the flat majority and reduces the number of messages the root receives. A design guide and a documentation audit of four Python frameworks translate these findings into implementation choices.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21259v1</id>
    <title>Evaluating Authorization and Trust Boundaries in Agentic Orchestration Frameworks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T15:33:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21259v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21259v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, and multi-agent collaboration, introducing security risks at orchestration boundaries. These risks depend on how identities are represented, operations are authorized, and instructions or information propagate between components. We evaluate LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen, and OpenClaw through twelve experiments mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications using a common LLM (gpt-4o-mini). The experiments cover prompt injection, unauthorized resource access and command execution, memory poisoning, and inter-agent trust and identity attacks. Adversarial inputs induced unauthorized tool invocation, while tool chaining, stale filesystem validation, encoded instructions, and inter-agent delegation exposed weaknesses in authorization across component boundaries. Memory poisoning showed that untrusted state can influence responses, a risk distinct from conventional access-control violations. In the evaluated protected configurations, explicit authorization, controlled capability assignment, filesystem containment, and execution safeguards prevented specific unauthorized operations. The findings emphasize preserving authorization and information-trust boundaries throughout agentic workflows rather than treating framework capabilities or model-level instructions as sufficient security guarantees.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17689v1</id>
    <title>Orbit-AWARE: From Onboard AI Deployment to Sustainable In-Orbit Intelligence</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T03:14:17Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17689v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17689v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The growing role of space computing in time-critical satellite services makes the long-term reliability of onboard artificial intelligence (AI) a mission-level requirement. Model drift can undermine this reliability through critical-observation suppression or noncritical priority flooding, displacing both mission information and evidence for model correction. To address this drift-induced evidence displacement, this article presents Orbit-AWARE, a safeguard-first lifecycle management (LCM) architecture. A comparison of existing approaches motivates cooperative Data, Cognitive, and Trust Planes for continuous monitoring, event-triggered agentic orchestration, and deterministic governance. The architecture retains a model-independent sample stream before degradation is confirmed and coordinates evidence selection and exchange for diagnosis and ground-assisted adaptation. Candidate updates are verified before control over data disposition is restored. In an xBD-based emergency Earth observation (EO) case study, Orbit-AWARE delivers 14.3\% more critical observations and achieves 8.3\% higher sustainable mission utility than the Rule-Based Drift Loop under a common 10\% downlink budget. Finally, we discuss future research directions for extending LCM through task-aware reliability assessment, memory- and tool-enabled onboard agents, and evidence-centric space networking. This work makes evidence availability and recovery authorization explicit design objectives for dependable onboard AI services.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16801v1</id>
    <title>Agentic Orchestration for SLA-Constrained Network Slicing in Programmable Mobile Data Planes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T13:42:36Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16801v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.16801v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Technical Specification 23.501 (Release 17) defines Maximum Bit Rate (MBR) enforcement at the User Plane Function (UPF) in fifth-generation (5G) networks. Supporting differentiated service-level agreements across the radio access and core networks requires the UPF to enforce MBR limits according to configured slice priorities. During overload, the challenge is to adapt these limits while preserving that differentiation and avoiding oscillations. Building on programmable enforcement and intelligent orchestration, we propose an agentic control loop combining UPF telemetry with locally hosted Large Language Model (LLM) selection from a finite set of admissible rate candidates. Deterministic logic validates each selection and derives Packet Forwarding Control Protocol (PFCP) updates. The evaluated runs show no oscillations or fallbacks and unchanged highest-priority rate limits. These observations establish configuration preservation; delivered per-class QoS protection remains unmeasured.</summary>
